rationale: Dropping unsolicited packets to stop port scans and flooding is resistance to network attacks.
Locking sign-in after repeated failures contains brute-force attempts (rule 1) and the text does not mention verifying credentials.
Preventing pages from reading or altering credential and profile files protects both confidentiality and integrity of that data.
Detecting whether stored records were altered since the last authorised write is an integrity check.
Only holders of the write privilege may create amendments, which restricts who can modify data (rule 3).
Restricting changes to templates to the chief physician limits who can modify data.
Idle-session termination limits misuse of an abandoned browser (rule 7), with no explicit data protection mentioned.
Validating the certificate chain and host name verifies that the site is who it claims to be.
Detecting tampering with model files and hostile input and falling back to a clean configuration is resistance and also covers integrity of the files.
Admitting a clinician only with a registered secret is password-based authentication.
Preventing users without admin rights from creating, editing or deleting records restricts modification; viewing is explicitly allowed.
Rejecting invalid values and keeping the dataset unchanged validates data accuracy and preserves integrity.
Requiring a passphrase before the email can be changed verifies the user and restricts modification of profile data.
Schema and checksum validation protects data accuracy, and blocking and flagging writes showing deliberate tampering is attack resistance.
Encrypting flight-plan updates so an eavesdropper cannot interpret them protects confidentiality (rule 5).
Requires users to prove identity with valid credentials, which is authentication.
Allowing payee-list changes only after explicit holder approval prevents unauthorised modification of data.
Only editors may trim, annotate or delete recordings, restricting who can modify data.
Preventing integrations from evading or disabling fraud-detection and brute-force protections preserves attack resistance.
Ensuring scripts cannot disable attack-detection and lockdown mechanisms keeps the software resistant to attack.
Accepting requests only from terminals that prove identity with a valid certificate is device authentication.
Verifying credentials against the stored account before access is authentication.
Verifying operator identity against the directory is authentication.
Encrypting travel documents so only the operator private key can decrypt them protects confidentiality.
Requires sign-in with an unshared individual account identifier, i.e. identifying each user before upload.
Verifying the origin of each feed with the source registered certificate is origin authentication.
Confirming the login secret matches the registered one is credential authentication.
Checking cached object files against recorded checksums and rejecting differing ones detects alteration of programs.
Detecting anomalous scanning traffic and blocking the source is intrusion detection and blocking.
Signing in with an identity assertion from a third-party identity provider is identity authentication.
Changes are limited to the owner (modification restriction) and require verified identity (authentication).
Hiding internal hosts and services from web pages prevents disclosure of internal network information, though it is not explicit whether an attack is being resisted.
Blocking unsolicited inbound internet traffic is a firewall defence against external attack.
Keeping the balance consistent and letting only authorised terminals change it protects data integrity.
Preventing pages and unapproved extensions from altering bookmarks and settings protects data from unauthorised modification.
A keyed HMAC tag with reporting of mismatches detects alteration of load-job files; origin verification is not stated.
Re-confirming identity through challenge questions before showing cards is identity verification.
Only data stewards may roll back a committed load, restricting who can modify data and restoring a consistent state.
Granting access only when the supplied identity matches a registered customer is authentication.
